text: Kazimierz Władysław Bartel (Polish pronunciation: [kaˈʑimjɛʐ vwaˈdɨswav ˈbartɛl]; English: Casimir Bartel; 3 March 1882 – 26 July 1941) was a Polish mathematician, freemason, scholar, diplomat, and politician who served as the 15th, 17th, and 19th Prime Minister of Poland three times between 1926 and 1930 and as a Senator of Poland from 1937 until the outbreak of World War II. He was appointed Minister of Railways between 1919 and 1920 and served as a member of Poland's Sejm from 1922 to 1929. After Józef Piłsudski's May Coup d'état in 1926, Bartel became prime minister for three non-consecutive terms: 1926, 1928–1929, and 1929–1930. During the period 1926–1928, he served as Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Religious Beliefs and Public Enlightenment, though he was effectively the de facto prime minister as Piłsudski did not engage in day-to-day government operations. In 1930, after stepping down from politics, Bartel returned to academia as a professor of mathematics at the Lwów Polytechnic and became its rector in 1930, receiving an honorary doctorate and membership in the Polish Mathematical Association. In 1937, he was appointed Senator of Poland and held that position until World War II began. After the Soviet invasion and occupation of eastern Poland, Bartel continued lecturing at the Technical Institute. In 1940, he was summoned to Moscow and offered a seat in the Soviet parliament. On 30 June 1941, during Operation Barbarossa, the German Wehrmacht entered Lwów and began persecuting the local intelligentsia. Bartel was imprisoned two days later by the Gestapo and offered the top post in a Polish puppet government; his refusal of these terms was deemed an act of treason by the Germans. By order of Heinrich Himmler, Bartel was murdered on 26 July 1941, shortly after the Massacre of Lwów professors ended. Bartel was born on 3 March 1882 in Lemberg, Austria-Hungary (later Lwów, Poland, now Lviv in Ukraine), the son of Michał Bartel and Amalia Chadaczek. Growing up in a working-class family, he graduated from elementary school in Stryj and, under his father’s guidance, became an apprentice to a fitter, allowing him to continue formal education. After completing secondary school in 1901, he studied mechanics at the Lwów Polytechnic in the Mechanical Engineering Department, graduating summa cum laude in 1907 and working as an assistant in descriptive geometry under Placyd Zdzisław Dziwinski. From 1908 to 1909, he studied mathematics and philosophy at the Franciscan University in Lviv and the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, where he attended lectures on art history by Karl Dochlemann and mathematics by Aurel Voss and Alfred Pringsheim. He returned to the Polytechnic and earned his doctor of technical sciences in 1909, with his dissertation "O utworach szeregów i pęków inwolucyjnych" making him one of the first to hold such a title in Austria-Hungary. He gave his habilitation thesis "O płaskich utworach inwolucji stopnia czwartego szeregu zerowego" in 1912 and was awarded the title of associate professor. He became chair of descriptive geometry in 1911 due to Mieczysław Łazarski’s blindness and attained the title of professor of mathematics in 1917. Conscripted into the Austro-Hungarian Army during World War I, Bartel returned to Lwów after the collapse of Austria-Hungary in 1918, which became part of the Second Polish Republic. In 1919, as commander of railway troops, he defended the city against the Ukrainian siege, wrote his first textbook on descriptive geometry, and befriended Józef Piłsudski, later supporting him. From 1919, he served as manager of the Armoured Trains Construction Management and Association, leading to his appointment as Minister of Railways by Prime Minister Leopold Skulski. After the Polish–Soviet War of 1920, he was nominated a lieutenant colonel and placed in charge of the railway reserve officers and the Lwów militia, receiving a Virtuti Militari cross for valor. In 1921, Bartel spent six months traveling to museums and galleries in France, Italy, Switzerland, and Austria to research art, amassing notes and photographs influenced by Dochlemann’s lectures. In 1922, he was elected to the Sejm and remained until 1929. Initially a member of the PSL "Liberation" party, he left in April 1925 due to its radicalization, joining with Marian Zyndram-Kościałkowski and Bolesław Wysłouch to form the parliamentary "Labour Club," which soon came under Piłsudski’s influence. Just before the May Coup of 1926, Bartel received an order from Marshal Piłsudski to prepare for a takeover as prime minister after President Stanisław Wojciechowski’s government collapsed. On 15 May 1926, after the resignation of Wincenty Witos’s government and President Wojciechowski, Bartel was appointed prime minister by Maciej Rataj, the acting head of state, though he stated in his speech that he would serve only until a new president was elected. This decision may have been due to his chronic kidney and stomach problems and constant pain. One parliament member noted that Bartel was cheerful and ambitious but always in pain, and although his opponents acknowledged his personal charm, his poor health and weak stature made him ineffective in public, especially among socialists or communists in the east, limiting his influence as a prime minister or diplomat. Bartel’s first government included mostly non-partisan members (four of whom already held ministerial positions) and was ideologically centrist, with both right-wing and left-wing leaders in the cabinet. Bartel himself took over the Ministry, while Piłsudski held the Ministry of War. This arrangement caused tension with the Polish Socialist Party, which supported the coup. On 16 May 1926, Bartel announced the government’s commitment to the rule of law, peace, hard work, and national dedication, and pledged to remove corrupt and incompetent officials. He advocated for a parliamentary system and emphasized fighting bureaucracy, creating an apolitical army, and eliminating the Ministry of Public Works. He stated that before the May Coup, Poland was ruled by an oligarchy of nobles and wealthy private clubs, not democracy. Supporters praised his efficiency in governance, while opponents accused him of undermining parliament and establishing a private "Sejm Bartlowy" (Bartel’s Parliament), where ministers reported directly to him. Bartel was seen as a liberal figure and a representative of the Sanacja movement. His government improved administration through strict organizational procedures: ministers had to submit all speeches and agendas to Bartel for approval, and ministers were prohibited from engaging in political activities. Bartel also worked to improve conditions for Polish Jews, opposing laws from the Tsarist era that persecuted religious minorities, and in 1927, his cabinet approved a law recognizing and granting rights to Jewish communities. On 2 August 1926, Parliament passed the "August Novella," significantly strengthening the president’s role. On 20 September 1926, the Christian Democratic Party voted against two ministers, Antoni Sujkowski and Kazimierz Młodzianowski, accusing them of political purges; the vote passed, forcing Bartel’s cabinet to resign. Marshal Piłsudski then ordered President Ignacy Mościcki to reappoint Bartel as prime minister. The change did not violate the Constitution, but it alarmed anti-parliamentarians and socialists, who threatened rebellion. Bartel’s third cabinet lasted only four days. On 30 September, at a meeting in the Belvedere palace, the council decided to dissolve the third government, requiring President Mościcki’s signature. Bartel informed Speaker Maciej Rataj that he would personally deliver the decree to Mościcki. After the Sejm passed the budget cut policy, Bartel went to Mościcki’s residence, but Mościcki refused to sign, instead ordering Bartel to terminate his employment. Bartel resigned again, but his cabinet remained intact and was replaced by Piłsudski himself. Bartel was deeply disappointed, despite having followed Piłsudski and Rataj’s plans. The Marshal warned that he would no longer compete with ministers and would use force if necessary. Following his resignation, Bartel became Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Religious Beliefs and Public Enlightenment in Piłsudski’s private council, acting as a substitute for the Marshal and as Speaker of the Sejm when absent. He frequently spoke on budget and financial matters, which were central to disputes between the "Piłsudskites" and the parliamentary opposition. After the March 1928 elections, Piłsudski intended to appoint Bartel as Speaker of the Sejm. On 27 March, the "Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government" (BBWR), closely aligned with Piłsudski, declared Bartel’s candidacy. However, the senators and members of parliament chose Ignacy Daszyński of the Polish Socialist Party as Marshal of the Sejm, prompting the BBWR members and supporters to leave the room in protest. In 1928, Bartel published his first book, "Perspektywa Malarska," on the theory of perspective and its application to architecture and art, published by Ksiaznica-Atlas in Lwów, with a German translation by B.G. Teubner in 1934. When a new government was formed without Bartel as head, Piłsudski temporarily served as prime minister and then decided to appoint Bartel, though it was only formal—Bartel already led the Council of Ministers. This decision angered senators, who boycotted sessions and even threw rotten food at departing ministers. The situation worsened, with demonstrators, often ordinary citizens acting on behalf of the party, physically abusing officials traveling to the government building on Wiejska Street in Warsaw. Similar incidents occurred during the inauguration of the first President of the Second Polish Republic, Gabriel Narutowicz, in December 1922. Ministers were advised to travel with guards or police.

When the new government was formed without Kazimierz Bartel as its head, Józef Piłsudski, who had temporarily served as Prime Minister, resigned, though he decided his position would be taken over by Bartel, considered his most trusted and loyal friend and supporter, even though this change was only formal—Bartel was already leading the Council of Ministers. This decision deeply angered the senators of parliament, who protested by refusing to attend sessions and even threw rotten food at departing ministers. The situation worsened as demonstrators, often ordinary citizens acting on behalf of the party, physically abused officials traveling to the government building on Wiejska Street in Warsaw. Similar incidents occurred during the inauguration of Gabriel Narutowicz, the first President of the Second Polish Republic, in December 1922. Politicians were advised to travel with guards or weapons for self-defense, though such measures might have intensified opposition and violence. In the so-called "Czechowicz affair," the opposition discovered that Chancellor Gabriel Czechowicz, a strong admirer of Piłsudski, diverted 8 million Polish złoty from the state budget to the BBWR campaign between 1927 and 1928. On 12 February 1929, members of an anti-Sanacja movement requested that both Czechowicz and Bartel be tried by the State Tribunal. In protest, Bartel announced his intention to resign and claimed the affair was caused by the Parliament and its senators, not a single politician. On 13 April 1929, Bartel ordered his government to resign, and was replaced by Kazimierz Świtalski, a stubborn and self-centered figure seen as a source of conflict with the opposition. Disputes between the new government and the Sejm continued, with Bartel’s cabinet beginning operations on 5 November 1929, though its first sitting occurred in December at the order of President Mościcki. The Parliament later passed a no-confidence motion against Świtalski’s cabinet, leading Bartel to become Prime Minister once again. On 29 December 1929, Bartel was chosen a third time and formed his fifth government, though he performed his duties under significant uncertainty due to poor health, including a kidney illness requiring ureterolithotomy with Tadeusz Pisarski and depression and anxiety from ongoing conflicts with the Sejm. On 10 January, he met with parliamentarians, declaring his willingness to cooperate, saying "I come with good will and determination gentlemen!" Initially, cooperation stabilized the situation, but relations deteriorated again, culminating in a no-confidence motion against Minister of Labour and Social Welfare Aleksander Prystor, initiated by the Polish Socialist Party led by Ignacy Daszyński and supported by Bolesław Limanowski, the oldest member of the Polish Senate until his death in 1935. On 12 March, Bartel delivered a sharp speech in the Senate, criticizing senators for failing to fulfill their duties and accusing them of stubbornness and pride that harmed the economy and state policies, stating that being a member of parliament is a profession requiring only obedience to the ruling party, not skill or damaging campaigns. He viewed the no-confidence motion as a lack of support from the government. On 15 March 1930, he resigned, and his resignation was accepted by the president the next day; he also resigned from parliament and left politics. Walery Sławek was appointed as the new prime minister. After retiring, Bartel returned to the Technical University of Lwów (Polytechnic), was elected rector for the 1930/1931 academic year, and received an honorary doctorate and membership in the Polish Academy of Sciences. From 1930 to 1932, he chaired the Polish Mathematical Society. During this time, he published his most important works, including a series of lectures on the perspective of European painting, the first of its kind globally. At the university, he opposed plans to introduce "ghetto benches" for Jewish students, leading to attacks such as eggs and rotten food being thrown at him or a pig with the sign "Bartel" being brought to the campus by Polish nationalists. In 1932, he testified in the Brest trials (26 October 1931 to 13 January 1932) at the Warsaw Regional Court, where leaders of the Centrolew, a centre-left anti-Sanacja movement, were tried. In 1937, Bartel was appointed Senator of Poland to replace Emil Bobrowski and served until the outbreak of World War II. In autumn 1938, he co-signed a document to President Mościcki calling for inclusion of opposition representatives in the government and for amnesty for opposition politicians imprisoned or exiled after the Brest trials; however, Mościcki did not respond. In February 1939, Bartel delivered a widely publicized speech in the Senate, sharply criticizing university conditions, widespread anti-Semitism, and poor academic organization. In September 1939, during the defense of Lwów before the German attack, Bartel served as head of the Civic Committee. After Lwów was occupied by the Soviet Union, he continued lecturing at the Technical University. In July 1940, he was summoned to Moscow, where he participated in an All-Committee meeting of Soviet universities. Discussions focused on scientific topics, and Bartel signed a contract with a publishing house to write a textbook on Science and Geometry for Soviet schools. He also visited institutions such as the Tretyakov Gallery and the Institute of Architecture. Some reports suggest the Soviets offered him political cooperation; according to close friends, Stalin proposed forming a new Polish government, which Bartel rejected. In a letter to his wife on 16 July 1941, he wrote: "By listening to private conversations of the officers, I conclude that my position as Prime Minister may be resurrected, but what great duty this will be to control a split, communist country. In Moscow with Joseph Stalin, I had the pleasure of finding out new information from the West—Winston Churchill's speech addressed to Władysław Sikorski about Poland's supposed future." One edition of "Paris' Historical Notebooks" described a letter to the German Ministry of Foreign Affairs stating that Reinhard Heydrich believed Bartel negotiated in early 1941 with the Soviets about establishing a new nation to declare war on Nazi Germany. A telegram from the Polish Chargé d’Affaires in Switzerland to London on 26 September 1940 stated: "It's believed that Moscow professor Bartel has intention to create the Red Government of Poland." This information was never proven. Maria Bartlowa, Bartel’s wife, stated he only discussed the release of his lecture book with the Soviets. It is widely believed he never met Stalin in person. Prime Minister-in-exile Władysław Sikorski had plans to cooperate with Bartel and appoint him ambassador, recognizing him as one of the few from the former political circles willing to cooperate under British conditions. On 19 June 1941, Sikorski officially reported Bartel’s candidacy during a Council of Ministers meeting, motivated by his political loyalty and efforts to preserve the Polish character of the Lwów Polytechnic under Soviet occupation. Sikorski failed to locate Bartel in the Soviet Union, and Stanisław Kot was appointed instead. On 30 June 1941, shortly after the German invasion of the Soviet Union, the Wehrmacht entered Lwów. Bartel was arrested on 2 July at a university meeting; thirty-six colleagues were arrested the next night. He was first held at a Gestapo prison on Pelczyńska Street, where he was treated well, allowed to receive and send letters, and bring food and mathematical books to his wife. On 21 July, he was transferred to a prison on Łąckiego Street, where he was mistreated; guards called him a "Commie-Jew," and Nazi officials ordered him to clean boots of a Ukrainian Hilfsgestapo soldier. According to Antoni Stefanowicz, Bartel was mentally devastated and could not comprehend the tragedy. Some sources claim Nazi officials proposed a Polish puppet government dependent on the Reich, as reported by Sikorski during a Cairo press conference in November 1941. According to his account, Bartel refused and was executed on 26 July 1941 at dawn, likely near Piaski Janowskie during the Massacre of Lwów professors. Bartel’s wife learned of his death on Monday, June 26, after being denied her regular food delivery on Saturday. One account states that on the night of October 1943, the Sonderkommando unearthed the mass grave of murdered Polish professors to remove evidence as Soviet troops approached. On 9 October 1943, the bodies were piled; prisoners were forced to take personal belongings, including documents of Bartel and Tadeusz Ostrowski. The pile was then set on fire, and the Sonderkommando scattered the ashes on surrounding fields. In 1966, on the 25th anniversary of the execution of the Lwów professors, a plaque listing the victims was placed at the church of St. Francis of Assisi in Kraków, with a separate epitaph honoring Bartel. Bartel’s wife saved his manuscript on perspective after his death by appealing to Nazi officials. His library was either shipped to Germany with furniture or burned with personal papers. Bartel’s second book was to be published first in German by B. G. Teubner, which would provide Ksiaznica-Atlas with negatives for the Polish edition. The war delayed printing and led to the destruction of all materials. In the 1950s, Professor F. Otto of the University of Gdansk reconstructed the book using surviving manuscripts and printer proofs sent by Teubner. It analyzed pictures geometrically, reconstructed geometric structures in art, and traced art history using Bartel’s theory of perspective. A uniform series was released by Polskie Wydawnictwo Naukowe, with the second volume in 1958 and the first volume in 1960. Bartel was decorated with the Order of the White Eagle (1932), the French Legion of Honour (class I), the Cross of Valour, the Cross of Independence, and the Silver Cross of the Virtuti Militari (1922).
